title: File systems, protection, virtual machines and contemporary systems
subtitle: How bytes become named files, how access is controlled, and how one machine pretends to be many.

sections.title: Files, directories and inodes
sections.body: A file is a named sequence of bytes with attributes (size, owner, permissions, times). Directories map names to files, forming a tree. On Unix-style systems the name points to an inode: a small record holding the attributes and the locations of the data blocks; the name itself is just an entry in a directory — which is why two names can reach one inode (a hard link).

questions.prompt: What does deleting one of two hard links to a file do?

choices.text: Turns the other link into a dangling pointer.
Removes one directory entry; the data stays until the link count reaches zero.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The other name still needs it.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: That is a symbolic link; hard links are equal peers.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The inode counts its names; only at zero are blocks freed.

sections.title: Allocating disk blocks
sections.body: Contiguous allocation is fast for sequential reads but fragments. Linked allocation chains blocks (FAT keeps the chain in a table) — no fragmentation, slow random access. Indexed allocation gives the file an index block (ext4/NTFS style, with extents) — fast random access at the cost of the index.

worked.why: An inode holds 12 direct pointers and one single-indirect block of 1024 pointers; blocks are 4 KB.
Direct data: 12 × 4 KB = 48 KB. Indirect: 1024 × 4 KB = 4 MB. Maximum without further levels:

questions.prompt: Which allocation method is best for random access?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Random access means walking the chain.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Block k is found by one index lookup; linked allocation must follow k pointers.

sections.title: Protection and security
sections.body: Authentication proves who you are (passwords, keys, multi-factor). Authorisation decides what you may do: an access-control list is stored with each object (who may touch me), a capability is held by each subject (what I may touch). Secure boot verifies each boot stage's signature; sandboxing confines a program to a restricted environment so a compromise stays small.

questions.prompt: An access-control list is attached to…

choices.text: The object (file/resource): it lists who may do what.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A capability list is attached to the subject instead.

diagram("mode: sequence
[User] as u
[Login service] as l
[Kernel] as k

sections.title: Hypervisors, VMs and containers
sections.body: A hypervisor lets several operating systems share one machine. Type 1 runs directly on hardware (Xen, ESXi, KVM); Type 2 runs as an application on a host OS (VirtualBox). A container (Docker) virtualises the operating system instead: containers share one kernel but see separate process, file and network namespaces — lighter and faster to start than a full VM, but with weaker isolation. Kubernetes schedules containers across many machines.

questions.prompt: Why does a container start faster than a VM?

choices.text: Containers are not isolated at all.
It has no guest kernel to boot — it shares the host’s.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: They are isolated by namespaces and cgroups, though less strongly than VMs.

figures.caption: Figure 7.1.1 — VM vs container
figures.note: A VM carries a whole OS; a container shares the host kernel.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
group "Virtual machines" { vm1, vm2, hyp }
group "Containers" { c1, c2, rt }
[Guest OS 1 + app] as vm1 #blue
[Guest OS 2 + app] as vm2 #blue
[Hypervisor] as hyp #violet
[Container A] as c1 #mint
[Container B] as c2 #mint
[Shared host kernel] as rt #violet
vm1 -> hyp
vm2 -> hyp
c1 -> rt
c2 -> rt");

sections.title: Windows, Linux, mobile, embedded, real-time
sections.body: Linux (monolithic, modular), Windows NT (hybrid kernel), Android (Linux kernel plus a managed runtime), iOS/macOS (XNU, a Mach–BSD hybrid). Embedded and IoT systems favour small real-time kernels (FreeRTOS, Zephyr); robots add middleware such as ROS; smart-cards run tiny, tightly secured systems. The same five concerns — processes, memory, files, I/O, protection — recur everywhere with different trade-offs.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Android applications run on a managed runtime above a Linux kernel.

problems.prompt: A 4 KB-block file system uses 12 direct and 1 single-indirect pointer (4-byte pointers). What is the largest file?
problems.answer: An indirect block holds 4096/4 = 1024 pointers. Total = (12 + 1024) × 4 KB = 4144 KB.

problems.prompt: Give one advantage and one risk of containers over VMs.
problems.answer: Advantage: start in milliseconds and use far less memory because they share the kernel. Risk: a kernel vulnerability affects every container on the host.
